name: Vaticinium ex eventu
statement: A prophecy composed after the events it claims to foretell, a verdict textual critics reach about a document rather than a measured tendency of minds.
meaning: The Latin means prophecy from the event. Böcher defines it, quoting Oßwald, as a feigned prophecy made on the basis of events that have already happened, and notes that vaticinium post eventum is sometimes used instead. Two parties stand behind any such text and only one of them is what the term describes. A writer who knows how something turned out puts that knowledge into the mouth of a figure placed earlier in time. Crabbe states the structure plainly: the prophecies describe events lying in the future from the perspective of the text and in the historical past from the perspective of its readers. The charge is about composition, and it attributes design rather than error. Scholars also use it as a dating tool. Segal gives the rule. Where a prophecy is correct across extensive details it was likely written after those events, and where it begins to diverge from what is known to have happened it was composed at the point where the divergence starts.

origin.note: The phrase was already settled scholarly Latin before this, and its coinage was not traced for this entry. Oßwald's article, "Zum Problem der Vaticinia ex eventu", volume 75, pages 27 to 44, is the earliest publication located that takes the category itself as its subject rather than applying it to a text. It was not obtained. Böcher's 1999 study of Revelation draws its definition from a later Oßwald reference article of 1966, cited there at column 2072. The reading the term supports is older than the term. Scolnic records that Porphyry, in the third century CE, identified the little horn of Daniel 7 as the Seleucid king Antiochus IV, that all modern scholars agree with him, and that many of Porphyry's interpretations are reported by Jerome.

evidence: The evidence is philological. Nobody has run a study; scholars argue case by case from the text and the historical record, and the strongest arguments turn on where a prediction stops being right. Segal calls Daniel 11 the best example in the entire Bible. Its account of dealings between the Ptolemies and the Seleucids is accurate through verse 39 and diverges at verse 40, which places the writing just after the events described up to that point. Scolnic reports that the consensus treating the book as a vaticinium ex eventu, written about 165 BCE as though foretold in the sixth century, has held for over a century since S. R. Driver's 1900 commentary, and that Daniel 7 to 12 is dated to the persecution of 167 to 164 and before Antiochus IV's death in 164 or 163. The same reading is applied well beyond Daniel. Böcher argues that the author of Revelation used the device repeatedly to structure his material, so that the catastrophes preceding salvation are retrospective interpretation of the present rather than genuine foretelling. Bracht notes that Hippolytus did not know Luke 21:20 was a vaticinium ex eventu, the Gospel of Luke having been written after 70 CE. Crabbe reads the prophecies in Books 1, 6 and 8 of the Aeneid the same way, including the parade of Roman figures Anchises shows Aeneas in the underworld at 6.752 to 892, in a poem written between Actium and Virgil's death in 19 BCE. Both writers name the same purpose. Correctly predicting what the reader already knows has happened buys credit for the predictions that remain outstanding, which Segal describes as raising the predictive value of the revelation in the reader's eyes. The category is not confined to antiquity. Böcher's opening example, from Peuckert, is a Silesian prophecy that claimed to date from 1630 and was in truth written in the early summer of 1813, covering Napoleon's campaign against Prussia in 1806 and 1807, the peace, and the coalition of 1813.

replication.headline: No empirical study of the term was found. It labels a compositional act by a writer, and nothing located turns it into a claim about people that could pass or fail.
replication.detail: Searches of Crossref, Europe PMC, arXiv and DOAJ return no experimental work on the phrase. Crossref's bibliographic index carries the term across theology, classics, Islamic studies and medieval literature, including Böcher on Revelation, Oßwald in 1963 and Pedersen in 1965 on the problem itself, Al-Azmeh on classical and medieval Muslim apocalyptic traditions, and a University of Toronto Press volume on retrospective prophecy in medieval English authorship. Europe PMC returns a single record, a paper on inflammation-associated proteins, and nothing on prophecy or judgement. A Crossref search pairing the phrase with hindsight bias returns the two literatures side by side and nothing joining them. The measured phenomenon nearest to it is hindsight bias, which is entry 48 here and has its own meta-analytic record. The two claims are not the same claim. Hindsight bias is about what a reader does with outcome knowledge once it arrives. Vaticinium ex eventu is about what a writer did with it on purpose, and no figure from the hindsight literature bears on whether a given passage was written before or after the event.

limits: The search covered Crossref by bibliographic query, Europe PMC, arXiv, DOAJ and general web search. OpenAlex refused the request for want of quota, and no theology-specific or classics-specific database such as ATLA or L'Année philologique was searched, so the absence of an empirical study is a statement about those places rather than about the whole literature. Several documents were named rather than read. Oßwald's 1963 article and Pedersen's 1965 article are behind paywalls and are cited from their Crossref records. Neujahr's 2012 monograph was not obtained; its chapter titles and pagination come from Crossref, and nothing here is drawn from its argument. Al-Azmeh's article and the Toronto volume were likewise not read beyond their bibliographic records. Böcher's article was read only as far as page 19, in Persée's automatic transcription, which Persée itself flags as uncorrected, so the definition and the Silesian example are secure and the rest of his argument is taken from the abstract Persée prints. The Peuckert 1941 article behind that example was not seen. Where a specific dating is quoted here it is one scholar's reading, not a settled quantity, and the underlying arguments are contested text by text.
misreadings: The most common error is the one that put this term on lists of cognitive biases at all. Wikipedia's article states that vaticinium ex eventu is a form of hindsight bias, files the page under Category:Cognitive biases, and carries no citation for that sentence; the article has been tagged as needing additional references since September 2014. A bias is something that happens to a judge without the judge intending it. The scholarly definitions say the opposite. Böcher's is a feigned prophecy, and Crabbe and Segal both describe an author arranging known history as prediction in order to win credit for what is still to come. Calling that a bias reads deliberate craft as an accident of memory. The second error is to treat the label as a neutral description that a text either fits or does not. It is a contested verdict. Scolnic notes that conservative scholars hold that part or all of Daniel 7 to 12 may go back to the sixth century rather than being vaticinia ex eventu, and den Hollander argues that the predictions attributed to Jesus about the fall of Jerusalem need not be dismissed as vaticinia ex eventu even by those who reject prophecy in principle, pointing to Borg's defence of their historicity. The third is to assume the charge implies fraud in the modern sense. It describes a recognised ancient literary form, used across Akkadian, Jewish, Christian, Greek, Roman, Muslim and medieval European writing, and the label says when a text was composed rather than what its author thought he was doing. The fourth is to import numbers. Hindsight bias has effect sizes and this does not, and no study located has assigned a rate or a magnitude to anything under this name.

sources.text: Böcher, O. (1999). Das beglaubigende Vaticinium ex eventu als Strukturelement der Johannes-Apokalypse. Revue d'histoire et de philosophie religieuses, 79(1), 19-30. Page 19 read in Persée's automatic transcription, which Persée flags as uncorrected; the German and French abstracts were read from the same record. Source for the definition, for the post eventum variant and for the 1813 Silesian prophecy.

Segal, M. (2021). The Four Kingdoms and Other Chronological Conceptions in the Book of Daniel. In A. B. Perrin & L. T. Stuckenbruck (Eds.), Four Kingdom Motifs before and beyond the Book of Daniel (pp. 13-38). Leiden: Brill. Open access, read in full. Source for the dating rule and for Daniel 11 being accurate through verse 39 and diverging at verse 40.

Crabbe, K. (2021). The Generation of Iron and the Final Stumbling Block: The Present Time in Hesiod's Works and Days 106-201 and Barnabas 4. In A. B. Perrin & L. T. Stuckenbruck (Eds.), Four Kingdom Motifs before and beyond the Book of Daniel (pp. 142-166). Leiden: Brill. Open access, read in full. Source for the definition quoted here and for the reading of the Aeneid.

Bracht, K. (2021). The Four Kingdoms of Daniel in Hippolytus's Commentary on Daniel. In A. B. Perrin & L. T. Stuckenbruck (Eds.), Four Kingdom Motifs before and beyond the Book of Daniel (pp. 167-190). Leiden: Brill. Open access, read in full. Source for the note on Hippolytus and Luke 21:20.

Scolnic, B. (2014). Antiochus IV and the Three Horns in Daniel 7. Journal of Hebrew Scriptures, 14, article 2. Read in full. Source for the consensus dating of Daniel, for the reference to S. R. Driver's 1900 commentary, for Porphyry and Jerome, and for the conservative dissent.

den Hollander, W. (2015). Jesus, Josephus, and the fall of Jerusalem: On doing history with Scripture. HTS Teologiese Studies / Theological Studies, 71(1), article 2942. Read in full in the SciELO South Africa text. Source for the argument that the sayings about Jerusalem need not be dismissed as vaticinia ex eventu, and for its citation of Borg.

Oßwald, E. (1963). Zum Problem der Vaticinia ex eventu. Zeitschrift für die Alttestamentliche Wissenschaft, 75(1), 27-44. Named as existing and as the source Böcher's definition descends from; not obtained, and its bibliographic details come from its Crossref record.

Pedersen, S. (1965). Zum Problem der vaticinia ex eventu. Studia Theologica - Nordic Journal of Theology. Cited as evidence that the category was treated as a problem in its own right in the 1960s; not obtained.

Neujahr, M. (2012). Predicting the Past in the Ancient Near East: Mantic Historiography in Ancient Mesopotamia, Judah, and the Mediterranean World. Providence: SBL Press. Not obtained. Cited for the reach of the category across its chapter titles, which Crossref gives as The Akkadian Ex Eventu Compositions at pages 13 to 74, Daniel and 1 Enoch at 119 to 152, Ex Eventu Prediction in the Dead Sea Scrolls at 153 to 194, and Ex Eventu Prediction in Greek Dress at 195 to 242.

Al-Azmeh, A. (2004). God's Chronography and Dissipative Time: Vaticinium ex Eventu in Classical and Medieval Muslim Apocalyptic Traditions. The Medieval History Journal, 7(2), 199-225. Not obtained; cited from its Crossref record for the term's use outside biblical studies.

Henry IV and the Ex Post Facto Construction of a Prophetic John Gower. In Retrospective Prophecy and Medieval English Authorship (pp. 70-103). University of Toronto Press, 2022. Not obtained; cited from its Crossref record, which carries no author, for the term's use in medieval literary studies.

Wikipedia, Vaticinium ex eventu. Used to find sources and quoted here as the carrier of the unsourced claim that the term is a form of hindsight bias, and for the page's categories and its September 2014 reference tag, read through the MediaWiki API. Not relied on for anything else.
